items.stem: Balance of payments data for Arvenia ($ bn): exports of goods 372; imports of goods 230; exports of services 103; imports of services 31; net primary income 4; net secondary income (transfers) 1. Calculate the balance of trade in goods and the balance of trade in services.
items.answer: Goods: 372 − 230 = $142 bn; services: 103 − 31 = $72 bn
items.markingKey: Goods 142; services 72. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for both balances. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant.

items.stem: Using the US current account deficit as an example, explain the link between the current and financial accounts.
items.answer: The USA has run a current account deficit every year since 1992, around 3-4% of GDP recently, financed by foreign purchases of US assets. The deficit is matched by a financial account surplus, as foreigners buy US bonds, shares and companies
items.markingKey: Context (The USA has run a current account deficit every year since 1992, around 3-4% of GDP recently, financed by foreign purchases of US assets.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Outline one way in which remittances to the Philippines shows the structure of the current account.
items.answer: Personal remittances to the Philippines were about $39 bn in 2023, around 9% of GDP. Remittances are secondary income credits that offset much of the Philippines' goods trade deficit
items.markingKey: Context (Personal remittances to the Philippines were about $39 bn in 2023, around 9% of GDP.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that a current account deficit is always a problem for an economy.
items.answer: A deficit is a problem when it is large, persistent and financed by short-term borrowing for consumption, not when it reflects productive investment financed by FDI.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: implies growing foreign debt; may reflect lack of competitiveness; vulnerable to sudden stops of capital. Arguments against: may reflect high investment that raises future capacity; financed by FDI is more sustainable; USA has run deficits for decades. Supported judgement: A deficit is a problem when it is large, persistent and financed by short-term borrowing for consumption, not when it reflects productive investment financed by FDI.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "current account".
items.answer: The part of the balance of payments recording trade in goods and services, primary income (wages, interest, profits, dividends) and secondary income (current transfers)

items.stem: Briefly explain why an inflow of foreign direct investment can later worsen the current account.
items.answer: Foreign-owned firms repatriate profits and dividends, which are debits in primary income on the current account.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Foreign-owned firms repatriate profits and dividends, which are debits in primary income on the current account. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between primary income and secondary income.
items.answer: Primary income is a return to factors of production (wages, interest, profits); secondary income is transfers with nothing given in return (remittances, aid).
items.markingKey: Primary income is a return to factors of production (wages, interest, profits); secondary income is transfers with nothing given in return (remittances, aid). items.stem: Define the term "expenditure-reducing policies".
items.answer: Contractionary fiscal and monetary policies that reduce AD and hence spending on imports

items.stem: A student claims that any current account deficit should be eliminated as quickly as possible. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Rapid correction via contractionary policy can cause recession; a modest deficit financed by FDI for productive investment can be sustainable.
items.markingKey: Rapid correction via contractionary policy can cause recession; a modest deficit financed by FDI for productive investment can be sustainable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why supply-side policies may be the best long-term way to correct a current account deficit.
items.answer: They raise productivity and quality, improving non-price and price competitiveness of exports without reducing growth. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They raise productivity and quality, improving non-price and price competitiveness of exports without reducing growth. items.stem: With reference to the Asian financial crisis of 1997, explain how it illustrates the risks of financing deficits with short-term capital.
items.answer: Thailand had current account deficits of about 8% of GDP in 1995-96, financed by short-term borrowing; when capital fled in 1997 the baht collapsed. A sudden stop forced a sharp currency depreciation and recession
items.markingKey: Context (Thailand had current account deficits of about 8% of GDP in 1995-96, financed by short-term borrowing; when capital fled in 1997 the baht collapsed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A sudden stop forced a sharp currency depreciation and recession – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the risks of financing deficits with short-term capital.

items.stem: Briefly describe Germany's current account surplus and explain what it reveals about consequences of persistent surpluses.
items.answer: Germany's current account surplus peaked at about 8.6% of GDP in 2015, drawing criticism from the IMF, the EU Commission and the US government. High saving and weak domestic investment created surpluses that contributed to global imbalances
items.markingKey: Context (Germany's current account surplus peaked at about 8.6% of GDP in 2015, drawing criticism from the IMF, the EU Commission and the US government.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: High saving and weak domestic investment created surpluses that contributed to global imbalances – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to consequences of persistent surpluses.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that depreciation of the currency is the most effective way to reduce a current account deficit.
items.answer: Depreciation can help in the short to medium term, but lasting correction requires supply-side improvements in competitiveness.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: makes exports cheaper and imports dearer; does not directly reduce growth; works if Marshall-Lerner holds. Arguments against: J-curve: short-run worsening; imported inflation; competitors may retaliate; does not fix non-price competitiveness. Supported judgement: Depreciation can help in the short to medium term, but lasting correction requires supply-side improvements in competitiveness.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "expenditure-switching policies".
items.answer: Policies, such as depreciation or protection, that switch spending from imports to domestically produced goods

items.stem: Explain the difference between expenditure-reducing policies and expenditure-switching policies.
items.answer: Expenditure switching changes the composition of spending away from imports (depreciation, tariffs); expenditure reducing lowers total spending, including on imports (contractionary fiscal or monetary policy).
items.markingKey: Expenditure switching changes the composition of spending away from imports (depreciation, tariffs); expenditure reducing lowers total spending, including on imports (contractionary fiscal or monetary policy). items.stem: Alessia writes: "A depreciation always improves the current account because exports become cheaper." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: If demand is price inelastic (PEDx + PEDm < 1), the fall in export prices and rise in import prices reduce net revenue, worsening the current account.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the UK devaluation of 1967 shows the J-curve.
items.answer: After the pound was devalued by 14.3% in November 1967, the UK current account worsened in 1968 before moving into surplus in 1969-1971. Inelastic short-run demand meant the balance worsened first, then improved as volumes adjusted
items.markingKey: Context (After the pound was devalued by 14.3% in November 1967, the UK current account worsened in 1968 before moving into surplus in 1969-1971.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Research by Montego's central bank finds PEDx = 1.1 and PEDm = 0.6 (absolute values). Using the Marshall-Lerner condition, explain whether a depreciation of the currency would improve the current account.
items.answer: PEDx + PEDm = 1.1 + 0.6 = 1.7. This is greater than 1, so the condition is satisfied: a depreciation should improve the current account (after any J-curve delay).
items.markingKey: [M1] sum of elasticities = 1.7; [A1] comparison with 1; [R1] explanation of why revenue/spending changes; [R1] J-curve/time caveat.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that a depreciation will always improve a country's current account in the long run.
items.answer: In most diversified economies the Marshall-Lerner condition holds in the long run, but the improvement may be small and temporary if inflation erodes the competitive gain.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: elasticities rise over time; empirical evidence for many countries; J-curve eventually turns up. Arguments against: commodity exporters face inelastic world demand; imported inflation erodes competitiveness; quality and non-price factors matter; trading partners may retaliate. Supported judgement: In most diversified economies the Marshall-Lerner condition holds in the long run, but the improvement may be small and temporary if inflation erodes the competitive gain.

items.answer: The Marshall-Lerner condition states when a depreciation will improve the current account (PEDx + PEDm > 1); the J-curve describes the time path, with an initial worsening before improvement as elasticities rise.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that developing countries should reduce their dependence on primary commodity exports.
items.answer: Diversification is desirable over time, but commodity revenues managed well (stabilisation funds, investment in education) can finance it.

items.markingKey: Context (Australia's terms of trade roughly doubled between 2003 and 2011 as China's demand for iron ore and coal soared.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Kwame writes: "A current account deficit means a country has an overall balance of payments deficit." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The BoP as a whole always balances; a current account deficit is matched by surpluses on the capital and financial accounts.
items.markingKey: The BoP as a whole always balances; a current account deficit is matched by surpluses on the capital and financial accounts. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Germany's current account surplus shows consequences of persistent surpluses.
items.answer: Germany's current account surplus peaked at about 8.6% of GDP in 2015, drawing criticism from the IMF, the EU Commission and the US government. High saving and weak domestic investment created surpluses that contributed to global imbalances
items.markingKey: Context (Germany's current account surplus peaked at about 8.6% of GDP in 2015, drawing criticism from the IMF, the EU Commission and the US government.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: High saving and weak domestic investment created surpluses that contributed to global imbalances – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to consequences of persistent surpluses.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the US dollar depreciation after 1985 shows the J-curve and Marshall-Lerner condition.
items.answer: After the Plaza Accord in 1985 the dollar fell sharply, but the US trade deficit kept widening until 1987 before narrowing. The delayed improvement suggests elasticities were low in the short run and higher later
items.markingKey: Context (After the Plaza Accord in 1985 the dollar fell sharply, but the US trade deficit kept widening until 1987 before narrowing.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The delayed improvement suggests elasticities were low in the short run and higher later – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the J-curve and Marshall-Lerner condition.

items.stem: Outline one way in which oil importers in 2022 shows a deterioration in the terms of trade.
items.answer: When oil prices rose above $100 a barrel in 2022, oil-importing countries such as India and Pakistan faced a deterioration in their terms of trade. Higher import prices meant more exports were needed to pay for the same imports, worsening the current account
items.markingKey: Context (When oil prices rose above $100 a barrel in 2022, oil-importing countries such as India and Pakistan faced a deterioration in their terms of trade.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Higher import prices meant more exports were needed to pay for the same imports, worsening the current account – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a deterioration in the terms of trade.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "A current account deficit is always a problem for an economy."
items.answer: A deficit is a problem when it is large, persistent and financed by short-term borrowing for consumption, not when it reflects productive investment financed by FDI.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: implies growing foreign debt; may reflect lack of competitiveness; vulnerable to sudden stops of capital. Arguments against: may reflect high investment that raises future capacity; financed by FDI is more sustainable; USA has run deficits for decades. Supported judgement: A deficit is a problem when it is large, persistent and financed by short-term borrowing for consumption, not when it reflects productive investment financed by FDI.

items.answer: Depreciation can help in the short to medium term, but lasting correction requires supply-side improvements in competitiveness.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that a depreciation will always improve a country's current account in the long run?
items.answer: In most diversified economies the Marshall-Lerner condition holds in the long run, but the improvement may be small and temporary if inflation erodes the competitive gain.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: elasticities rise over time; empirical evidence for many countries; J-curve eventually turns up. Arguments against: commodity exporters face inelastic world demand; imported inflation erodes competitiveness; quality and non-price factors matter; trading partners may retaliate. Supported judgement: In most diversified economies the Marshall-Lerner condition holds in the long run, but the improvement may be small and temporary if inflation erodes the competitive gain. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "primary income".
items.answer: Income from factors of production: compensation of employees, interest, profits and dividends received from or paid abroad

items.stem: A disadvantage of using contractionary fiscal policy to reduce a current account deficit is that it:
items.answer: reduces growth and increases unemployment

items.stem: Distinguish between the terms of trade and the balance of trade.
items.answer: The terms of trade is a ratio of export to import prices; the balance of trade is the value of exports minus the value of imports (prices × volumes).
items.markingKey: The terms of trade is a ratio of export to import prices; the balance of trade is the value of exports minus the value of imports (prices × volumes). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the current account and the financial account.
items.answer: The current account records trade in goods and services and income flows; the financial account records flows of investment (direct, portfolio) and reserves.
items.markingKey: The current account records trade in goods and services and income flows; the financial account records flows of investment (direct, portfolio) and reserves. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between expenditure-reducing policies and expenditure-switching policies.
items.answer: Expenditure switching changes the composition of spending away from imports (depreciation, tariffs); expenditure reducing lowers total spending, including on imports (contractionary fiscal or monetary policy).
items.markingKey: Expenditure switching changes the composition of spending away from imports (depreciation, tariffs); expenditure reducing lowers total spending, including on imports (contractionary fiscal or monetary policy). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Marshall-Lerner condition and the J-curve.
items.answer: The Marshall-Lerner condition states when a depreciation will improve the current account (PEDx + PEDm > 1); the J-curve describes the time path, with an initial worsening before improvement as elasticities rise.
items.markingKey: The Marshall-Lerner condition states when a depreciation will improve the current account (PEDx + PEDm > 1); the J-curve describes the time path, with an initial worsening before improvement as elasticities rise. items.stem: Briefly describe Sri Lanka's current account and reserves crisis and explain what it reveals about consequences of current account deficits.
items.answer: Sri Lanka's large current account deficits and falling tourism after 2019 drained foreign reserves to almost zero by 2022. Without capital inflows to finance the deficit, the country could not pay for essential imports and defaulted
items.markingKey: Context (Sri Lanka's large current account deficits and falling tourism after 2019 drained foreign reserves to almost zero by 2022.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Without capital inflows to finance the deficit, the country could not pay for essential imports and defaulted – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to consequences of current account deficits.

items.stem: Briefly describe the UK devaluation of 1967 and explain what it reveals about the J-curve.
items.answer: After the pound was devalued by 14.3% in November 1967, the UK current account worsened in 1968 before moving into surplus in 1969-1971. Inelastic short-run demand meant the balance worsened first, then improved as volumes adjusted
items.markingKey: Context (After the pound was devalued by 14.3% in November 1967, the UK current account worsened in 1968 before moving into surplus in 1969-1971.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: "Any current account deficit should be eliminated as quickly as possible." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Rapid correction via contractionary policy can cause recession; a modest deficit financed by FDI for productive investment can be sustainable.
items.markingKey: Rapid correction via contractionary policy can cause recession; a modest deficit financed by FDI for productive investment can be sustainable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the J-curve effect following a depreciation.
items.answer: Current account balance (y-axis) against time; depreciation at t0; the balance first worsens because demand is price inelastic in the short run (existing contracts), then improves as elasticities rise, forming a J shape.
